cls: Synthetic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) analog (diagnostic and therapeutic corticotropin)
pharm: A synthetic polypeptide corresponding to the first 24 amino acids of human ACTH (corticotropin) that stimulates the adrenal cortex to secrete cortisol, corticosterone, and androgens; used diagnostically to assess adrenocortical reserve (short Synacthen test) and therapeutically (depot form) in certain inflammatory, rheumatic, and seizure disorders.

No specific interaction; corticosteroid effects (e.g., GI) may be relevant with chronic depot use
Cortisol response (diagnostic); BP, glucose, electrolytes, infection signs (therapeutic depot)
summary: Tetracosactide (also called tetracosactrin; brand Synacthen) is a synthetic analog of corticotropin (ACTH) comprising the biologically active first 24 amino acids of natural ACTH. It is the cosyntropin analog - cosyntropin (Cortrosyn) is the equivalent agent used in the United States. By binding adrenal melanocortin receptors it stimulates the adrenal cortex to release cortisol and other steroids. Its main use is diagnostic: the short Synacthen test assesses adrenal insufficiency, with a standard 250 microgram dose given IV or IM and serum cortisol measured before and after. A long-acting depot formulation is used therapeutically in some regions for inflammatory and rheumatic conditions and for infantile spasms (West syndrome). It is not FDA-approved as Synacthen in the US.
indications: Diagnostic assessment of adrenocortical function - short Synacthen (ACTH stimulation) test for suspected adrenal insufficiency
Therapeutic use (depot formulation) in certain inflammatory and rheumatic disorders where corticotropin therapy is indicated
Treatment of infantile spasms (West syndrome) in some regions (depot formulation)

dosage.d: 250 micrograms as a single dose; measure serum cortisol at baseline and typically 30 (and/or 60) minutes after
dosage.n: Adequate response indicates intact adrenal function

dosage.d: Often 250 micrograms in older children; lower/weight-based doses used in infants per protocol
Individualized; e.g., 1 mg depot given intermittently per regional product information, titrated to response

admin: For the short test, give 250 micrograms by IV or IM injection and draw serum cortisol at baseline and at 30 (and/or 60) minutes
The depot (long-acting) formulation is given by intramuscular injection only - never give the depot intravenously
Have facilities to manage hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis available, particularly in atopic or allergic patients
For therapeutic depot use, apply corticosteroid-type precautions (infection, glucose, BP, electrolytes)
Individualize therapeutic dosing to clinical response and taper appropriately
moa: Tetracosactide is a synthetic peptide reproducing the N-terminal 1-24 amino acid sequence of human ACTH (corticotropin), which carries the full corticotropic activity of the natural hormone. It binds melanocortin type 2 receptors on adrenocortical cells, activating adenylate cyclase and increasing cyclic AMP, which stimulates the synthesis and release of glucocorticoids (chiefly cortisol), mineralocorticoids, and adrenal androgens. Diagnostically, the resulting rise in serum cortisol reflects adrenocortical reserve; therapeutically, the increased endogenous corticosteroid output mediates anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects.

absolute: Allergic disorders such as asthma in some labeling (risk of severe hypersensitivity)
Acute psychosis, infectious conditions, peptic ulcer, and other classic corticotropin/corticosteroid contraindications (therapeutic use)
Refractory heart failure, Cushing's syndrome, and certain endocrine disorders (per product information)
relative: Atopy / history of allergic disease (heightened hypersensitivity risk)
Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, osteoporosis (corticosteroid effects with therapeutic use)
monitor: Blood pressure, blood glucose, and electrolytes (therapeutic)
Signs of infection and corticosteroid adverse effects (therapeutic)

preg: Use during pregnancy only if clearly necessary and under specialist guidance. As tetracosactide raises endogenous corticosteroid levels, the considerations applicable to corticosteroid exposure in pregnancy apply; the single diagnostic dose is generally a lesser concern than prolonged therapeutic depot use.
lact: Data on use during breastfeeding are limited. The decision to use, particularly the therapeutic depot form, should weigh the clinical need against limited safety information under specialist guidance.
renal: No specific, well-established dose adjustment is defined for renal impairment. Use with caution and apply corticosteroid-related monitoring (fluid balance, electrolytes) for therapeutic use.
hepatic: No specific, well-established dose adjustment is defined for hepatic impairment. Use with caution and monitor as appropriate for therapeutic (depot) corticotropin use.

major: Live vaccines - corticosteroid-like immunosuppression with therapeutic use may reduce response/increase risk; avoid
Drugs that affect adrenal steroid synthesis (e.g., metyrapone, glucocorticoids, estrogens) - can confound the cortisol test result
moderate: Concurrent corticosteroids - additive corticosteroid effects and may invalidate diagnostic testing
Antidiabetic agents - corticosteroid-induced hyperglycemia may reduce their effect (therapeutic use)
Potassium-depleting agents / diuretics - additive hypokalemia risk (therapeutic use)
Anticoagulants - corticosteroid effects may alter response; monitor
minor: No clinically significant minor interactions well characterized
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; corticosteroid-related gastrointestinal effects may be relevant with prolonged therapeutic use.
interactions.diagnostics: Exogenous glucocorticoids, estrogens, and adrenal-acting drugs can alter baseline and stimulated cortisol; spironolactone and certain assays can interfere with cortisol measurement - interpret the test accordingly.

common: Effects related to raised corticosteroids with repeated dosing
serious: Corticosteroid adverse effects with prolonged use (hyperglycemia, hypertension, hypokalemia, osteoporosis, infection risk, mood changes)
Adrenal suppression with prolonged therapeutic use
rare: Severe allergic/anaphylactoid reaction (more likely in atopic patients)
Cushingoid changes with prolonged depot therapy
emergency: Acute adrenal crisis on abrupt withdrawal after prolonged use

monitoring: Serum cortisol at baseline and post-stimulation (diagnostic test)
Watch for immediate hypersensitivity after injection, especially in atopic patients
Blood pressure, blood glucose, and electrolytes during therapeutic depot use
Signs of infection and corticosteroid adverse effects with prolonged use
counsel: For the adrenal (Synacthen) test, a blood sample is taken before and after the injection to measure your cortisol response
Tell the team about any allergies or asthma - allergic reactions can occur after the injection
If you are receiving the long-acting (depot) form for treatment, do not stop it abruptly and report infections, mood changes, swelling, or high blood sugar
Report rash, swelling, breathing difficulty, or dizziness immediately after an injection
This agent is the cosyntropin analog; in the US, cosyntropin (Cortrosyn) is the equivalent product used
pk: Plasma cortisol begins to rise within minutes; clear increase typically by ~30 minutes (short test)
Stimulated cortisol generally peaks around 30-60 minutes after the standard 250 microgram dose
Tetracosactide is rapidly cleared (short plasma half-life); the depot formulation prolongs the duration of effect
Short-acting (aqueous) effect lasts a few hours; depot (zinc) formulation acts for a prolonged period (hours to ~1-2 days)
Store refrigerated (2-8 C); protect from light per product information
pearls: Tetracosactide is a cosyntropin analog (synthetic ACTH 1-24); in the US, cosyntropin (Cortrosyn) is the equivalent product - Synacthen is not FDA-approved in the US
Standard short Synacthen / ACTH stimulation test uses 250 micrograms IV or IM with cortisol measured at baseline and ~30 (and/or 60) minutes to assess adrenal insufficiency
Depot (long-acting) form is used therapeutically for some inflammatory/rheumatic conditions and for infantile spasms (West syndrome) in some regions - give IM only, never IV
Hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis, can occur - be especially cautious in atopic/allergic patients and have resuscitation facilities available
Prolonged therapeutic use produces corticosteroid-type effects and adrenal suppression - apply corticosteroid precautions and avoid abrupt withdrawal
missed: The short diagnostic test is a single dose, so a missed dose is not applicable - the test is simply rescheduled. For therapeutic depot dosing, follow the prescriber's instructions for a missed injection and do not give extra to make up; do not stop prolonged therapy abruptly.
overdose: Overdose or excessive/prolonged dosing produces exaggerated corticosteroid effects (fluid retention, hypertension, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, cushingoid features) and may cause adrenal suppression. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with monitoring and correction of fluid/electrolyte and glucose abnormalities, and appropriate management of any hypersensitivity reaction.
